enums.name: OccurrenceLevel
enums.description: Five-level likelihood of the (random) fault that the monitoring is meant to guard against, over the product service life. Level 1 = low occurrence of random faults; Level 5 = high occurrence of random faults. Rated on the fault itself, independent of the monitor.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — Very Low: random fault very unlikely; robust, proven design with a very low random failure rate
Level 2 — Low: random fault unlikely; established design with a low failure rate
Level 3 — Medium: random fault plausible; moderate failure rate
Level 4 — High: random fault likely; elevated failure rate
Level 5 — Very High: random fault very likely; high random failure rate

enums.name: DetectionLevel
enums.description: Five-level capability of the runtime monitoring to detect the fault. Level 1 = high detection capability; Level 5 = low detection capability.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — High capability: the failure modes across the different operating conditions are detected with high confidence (e.g. a diverse sensor of similar accuracy, so a narrow delta band can be monitored and deviations detected)
Level 2 — Good capability: most failure modes detected across the main operating conditions, with some conditions less well covered
Level 3 — Moderate capability: the common failure modes are detected under nominal conditions; corner cases and some operating conditions may be missed
Level 4 — Limited capability: only a subset of failure modes detected, under specific conditions
Level 5 — Low capability: a simple plausibility check that catches only some failure modes

sections.title: Question 1: Is the monitored fault clearly defined?
paragraphs: Each monitoring entry should reference a specific fault (or failure mode) it is meant to detect, and the element it occurs at.
The occurrence rating reflects how likely that (random) fault is over the service life — independent of the monitor.
The following list of common electrical/electronic failure modes is a starting point — select the **relevant** ones per monitored element rather than applying all of them.

sections.title: Question 2: Is the detection capability justified?
paragraphs: The detection rating reflects the capability of the runtime monitoring. A simple plausibility check that catches only some failure modes is a low capability; detecting the failure modes across the different operating conditions with high confidence (for example a diverse sensor of similar accuracy where a narrow delta band is monitored and deviations are detected) is a high capability.
State the independence of the monitor from the monitored function so a single cause cannot defeat both.

sections.title: Question 3: Is the system response defined?
paragraphs: On detection, what does the system do (e.g. enter the safe state, degrade, notify the operator)? The response is what turns a potential single-point fault into a monitored one.

sections.title: Question 4: Are the tasks managed?
paragraphs: If additional monitoring, independence measures, or verification are required, a ticket shall be created to manage the task.

items.name: Loss of function / no output
items.description: The device or one of its functional channels stops providing its intended result. Examples include a camera producing no image, a sensor providing no measurement, or an actuator producing no movement, force, pressure, or flow.
items.measures: Use alive monitoring, heartbeat, update-rate supervision, supply monitoring, or observation of the expected downstream effect. Detect the loss within the fault-tolerant time interval and define a degraded or safe reaction.

items.name: Degraded sensing / transduction
items.description: The sensing path still operates but loses sensitivity, resolution, contrast, dynamic range, or coverage. Examples include dead or hot image pixels, reduced detector sensitivity, damage or misalignment in an electro-optical path, or degradation of an electrical, acoustic, pressure, or position transducer.
items.measures: Monitor signal quality indicators, calibration references, usable range, bad-channel counts, image-quality metrics, or agreement with a diverse sensor or physical model. Define limits beyond which the measurement is no longer trusted.

items.name: Measurement drift / bias
items.description: The reported value gradually shifts from the true value because of ageing, temperature cycling, humidity-related electrical degradation, reference drift, calibration loss, or sensor wear, while remaining superficially plausible.
items.measures: Perform reference or zero-point checks, monitor long-term trends, compare redundant or diverse measurements, and apply model-based plausibility checks. Recalibrate or reject the channel when drift exceeds its tolerance.

items.name: Noisy / intermittent output
items.description: The device output contains excessive noise, dropouts, flicker, sporadic invalid samples, or unstable connections. The fault may appear only at certain temperatures, vibration levels, loads, or operating conditions.
items.measures: Monitor variance, dropout rate, invalid-sample count, discontinuities, and connection health over a time window. Avoid masking a recurring fault with filtering alone; latch or escalate the diagnostic when recurrence exceeds a threshold.

items.name: Incorrect internal processing
items.description: The processor executes the intended processing incorrectly because runtime hardware is degraded or corrupted. Examples include wrong image processing, filtering, colour correction, focus evaluation, sensor fusion, control calculation, or output encoding despite valid inputs.
items.measures: Use end-to-end plausibility checks, reasonableness checks on intermediate and final results, control-flow or lock-step monitoring, and independent calculation for safety-critical results. This mode concerns random execution faults, not a systematic defect in the designed algorithm.

items.name: Memory / internal state corruption
items.description: Working data, calibration data, configuration, program memory, or internal state becomes corrupted or is lost, leading to incorrect processing, wrong operating mode, invalid calibration, or unpredictable output.
items.measures: Protect memory and stored data with ECC, parity, CRC, redundant storage, range checks, and periodic read-back or scrubbing. Reinitialize to a validated state or enter a safe state when integrity cannot be restored.

items.name: Timing / clock fault
items.description: Internal timing is lost or becomes inaccurate because a clock stops, drifts, becomes unstable, or loses synchronization. Processing or actuation may then be too late, too early, irregular, or performed at the wrong rate.
items.measures: Use an independent clock supervisor, window watchdog, deadline monitoring, timestamp/rate checks, or comparison with a second time base. Define the reaction to clock loss, excessive drift, or missed deadlines.

items.name: Power supply degradation / interruption
items.description: Internal or supplied power is absent, intermittent, noisy, or outside its valid voltage/current range. The device may reset, operate unpredictably, lose performance under load, or disable only part of its sensing, processing, or actuation chain.
items.measures: Monitor relevant rails for under-voltage, over-voltage, ripple, brown-out, and unexpected reset. Supervise current where useful and hold outputs in a defined safe state outside the valid supply window.

items.name: Loss of internal actuation
items.description: An integrated motor, solenoid, pump, valve, positioning stage, or similar electrically commanded mechanism does not move or generate the requested force, pressure, or flow. Examples include a camera focus motor that no longer moves or an electrohydraulic valve that does not respond.
items.measures: Compare commanded and measured position, speed, current, pressure, force, or flow. Detect lack of response, excessive current, timeout, or failure to reach the commanded state and transition to a defined fallback.

items.name: Degraded / inaccurate actuation
items.description: An integrated actuator still responds but is slow, weak, inaccurate, oscillatory, or unable to hold its commanded state because of ageing or degradation in its motor, driver, feedback sensor, valve, pump, or transmission path.
items.measures: Monitor tracking error, response time, settling time, current or pressure signature, achieved force/flow, oscillation, and position stability. Trend these indicators so gradual degradation is detected before complete loss.

items.name: Internal feedback / regulation fault
items.description: An internal closed-loop function uses missing, biased, noisy, or stuck feedback and therefore regulates the wrong value or becomes unstable. Examples include autofocus, image stabilization, speed, position, voltage, temperature, or pressure control.
items.measures: Check command-to-feedback consistency, controller saturation, persistent control error, convergence, and oscillation. Where practical, compare feedback with an independent limit switch, sensor, or observable physical effect.

items.name: Internal communication / data-path fault
items.description: Data between sensing, processing, memory, and actuation stages is lost, delayed, frozen, corrupted, or assigned to the wrong channel, so individually healthy subfunctions no longer work together correctly.
items.measures: Use end-to-end CRC, sequence counters, freshness monitoring, timeout supervision, channel identifiers, and interface self-tests. Detect partial communication loss rather than relying only on an overall device heartbeat.

items.name: Transient upset (radiation / EMC / electrical disturbance)
items.description: A temporary disturbance corrupts logic, memory, sensing, communication, or control without necessarily causing permanent damage. Examples include a radiation-induced single-event upset, EMC-induced glitch, electrostatic discharge effect, or short supply disturbance.
items.measures: Use ECC/parity, retries, temporal plausibility checks, redundant execution, watchdog recovery, and controlled reinitialization. Count recurrences and escalate repeated transient events because they may indicate permanent degradation or an unsuitable environment.

items.name: Temperature-related functional degradation
items.description: The device remains powered but its sensing accuracy, processing reliability, communication, or actuation capability deteriorates at high or low temperature or after repeated thermal cycling and ageing.
items.measures: Monitor internal temperature and temperature-dependent quality/performance indicators. Apply validated compensation where possible and derate, disable, or enter a safe state outside the qualified operating range.

items.name: Missing output / no update
items.description: A measurement, message, or status is absent or stops updating although the function is expected to be active.

items.name: Stuck / frozen output
items.description: The output remains fixed or repeats old data even though the observed quantity or commanded state changes.

items.name: Incorrect / implausible output
items.description: The output is present but has a wrong value, sign, state, range, or physical relationship to other signals.

items.name: Drifting / biased output
items.description: The output changes gradually away from its correct value while remaining within a superficially valid range.

items.name: Noisy / intermittent interface
items.description: The interface exhibits excessive noise, glitches, sporadic dropouts, flicker, or unstable communication.

items.name: Timing / freshness failure
items.description: Data or response arrives too late, too early, irregularly, or with an invalid age, update rate, sequence, or timestamp.

items.name: Corrupted / incomplete data
items.description: The transferred data is altered, truncated, internally inconsistent, or accepted despite a failed integrity check.

items.name: Wrong channel / source assignment
items.description: A valid-looking signal or command belongs to the wrong sensor, actuator, redundant lane, or logical channel.

H.label: High
H.description: Highest priority. Requires a mitigation, or an explicit rationale for the current severity/occurrence/detection combination.

M.label: Medium
M.description: Moderate priority. Review the rating and consider whether further risk reduction is worthwhile.

L.label: Low
L.description: Lower priority given the current rating. Still subject to normal review.

enums.name: OccurrenceLevel
enums.description: Five-level classification of failure likelihood based on software component complexity.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — Very Low: simple, mostly stateless software with straightforward algorithms
Level 2 — Low: moderate algorithmic complexity with limited branching
Level 3 — Medium: some state management or multiple execution paths
Level 4 — High: complex state machines, event-driven behavior, complex dependencies
Level 5 — Very High: highly complex and highly stateful behavior

enums.name: DetectionLevel
enums.description: Five-level classification of detection capability for potential problems during development or runtime. Higher level = weaker detection capability.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — Proven: proven detection method, virtually certain to catch the defect before release (e.g. dedicated test or runtime monitoring to cover this specific scenario)
Level 2 — Good: automatic detection with high coverage (e.g. detected by static analysis, automated test suites with coverage of corner cases, covered by runtime measures like timing monitoring)
Level 3 — Moderate: semi-automatic or manual detection with moderate coverage (e.g. may be detected during integration testing, no runtime monitoring)
Level 4 — Limited: detection only under specific conditions; issues may escape to later phases
Level 5 — None: no detection opportunity or no control exists; latent failures possible

enums.name: TaskType
enums.description: Classification of the type of safety task.

permissibleValues.description: Safety measure implemented and active at runtime (e.g. monitoring, diagnostics, fault reaction)
Safety measure applied during development (e.g. review, analysis, testing, design constraint)
Other task type not covered by the standard categories

sections.title: Question 1: Analysis Input sufficient?
paragraphs: Does the SW Safety Analysis reflect the **current** SW Architecture? Are all SW components and interfaces of SW components listed in the Safety Analysis?
For each component SW Safety Analysis there should be a description of the main functions of that component.

sections.title: Question 2: Are all relevant failure modes for the SW covered?
paragraphs: The following list of potential failure modes does not need to be applied for every SW component analysis. Instead, the **relevant failure modes shall be selected per component**. For those which are related to the overall architecture, provide an argument (for example, regarding the risk that several components access shared resources, an exclusive lock is used).

sections.title: Question 3: Are the safety requirements linked?
paragraphs: The failure modes of an analysis should have a relation to the main SW Safety Requirements. For example, if a component does not execute the specified function, what is the Safety Requirement which is violated?
It is **NOT sufficient** to just select an ASIL — the requirement which is related to the ASIL shall be linked.

sections.title: Question 4: Is the risk rating performed?
paragraphs: For SW Safety Analysis there should be at least one risk rating documented describing the main aspects:
bullets: What is the **occurrence** of the failure scenarios?
What are the **measures to prevent** this from occurring?
Are **further measures required** to monitor this scenario during runtime?
sections.note: For interface failure modes it is NOT required to perform a risk rating. The risk rating is performed for the functional failure modes of a SW component.

sections.title: Question 5: Are the tasks managed?
paragraphs: If during the safety analysis risk reduction tasks are defined related to dedicated runtime measures (for example, additional plausibility checks) or development-time measures (for example, additional fault injection tests), then a ticket shall be created in the task tracking system to manage the tasks.

items.name: Concurrency failures
items.description: Incorrect concurrent access to shared resources across execution contexts (tasks, threads, ISRs, fibers, coroutines, processes, cores) causing race/data race, lost update, torn read/write, deadlock/livelock, priority inversion, or inconsistent lock ordering, resulting in corrupted shared state or incorrect behavior.
items.measures: Make the reentrancy contract of every function explicit: pure-reentrant (only stack/parameters), reentrant under lock, or non-reentrant (single-context only). For non-reentrant code, guarantee single-writer ownership and a single calling context (one task/thread/node on one core, no concurrent activation). For shared state, protect with the appropriate primitive for the platform (mutex, semaphore, spinlock, critical section, atomic, RCU, message queue) and define a documented lock order to avoid deadlock. Avoid non-reentrant library calls (errno, strtok, static buffers) in shared code paths.

items.name: Config & Calibration failures
items.description: Problems related to calibration and configuration data, e.g. wrong or missing calibration values, wrong configuration parameters (build-time, install-time, or runtime), unsafe default values, inconsistent parameter sets between modules.
items.measures: Store calibration/configuration data in protected memory with integrity checks (CRC/checksum). If parameters can change post-release (field calibration, ground station upload, fleet update), apply range and plausibility checks on load and at use. If calibration is fixed at development time, the review and test process is the primary mitigation. Define and validate safe defaults for the case where stored data is invalid or absent.

items.name: Debug/development functionality enabled
items.description: Development or test functionality remains enabled in the released software (e.g., diagnostic overrides, bypass switches, force values, test/maintenance modes, overly permissive safety gates, debug backdoors, calibration write access, verbose logging that affects timing), leading to unintended behavior in the field.
items.measures: Remove development functions from the production build, or guard them behind compile-time switches, signed/authenticated unlock, or hardware jumpers that are physically absent in the released configuration. Verify by build-artifact inspection and dedicated test cases.

items.name: Failure to activate / missing function
items.description: The software function fails to activate when required (e.g., missed trigger, suppressed transition, incorrect inhibit/enable logic, blocked event, dropped activation request).
items.measures: Component specific failure mode.

items.name: Fault handling / fallback failure
items.description: A safety mechanism detects a fault but the mitigation is incorrect or missing (unsafe default, no degraded/fail-operational/fail-safe mode, wrong fallback selection, fault not latched, fault masked by another).
items.measures: Component specific failure mode.

items.name: Incorrect control output (wrong value)
items.description: The computed output is incorrect due to algorithm or implementation error, including wrong magnitude, wrong sign, or wrong direction (e.g., wrong formula/branch/parameter usage; control assist inverted; actuator command sign or axis wrong; thrust/torque/force command incorrect).
items.measures: Component specific failure mode.

items.name: Initialization failures
items.description: Software function is not initialized as expected: variables/buffers not set up correctly, peripherals/drivers not configured, initialization sequence not followed, dependencies started in wrong order, partial init after warm restart.
items.measures: Cover application-level init by program-flow monitoring during startup. For code that runs before the OS/scheduler (boot, pre-OS self-tests, BSP), apply specific monitoring to ensure required hardware self-tests and platform checks complete before normal operation begins. Define and verify the init order across modules; assert preconditions at module entry.

items.name: Limit handling failure (saturation / clamp / rate limit)
items.description: Safety or physical limits are not applied correctly (missing saturation, wrong clamp bounds, rate limiter bypassed or wrongly sized, integrator wind-up), causing out-of-range, abrupt, or unstable outputs.
items.measures: Component specific failure mode.

items.name: Numeric robustness failure
items.description: Numeric issues such as integer overflow/underflow, divide-by-zero, NaN/Inf propagation, unintended type promotion, signed/unsigned mix, or wraparound counters cause incorrect outputs or transitions.
items.measures: Define the value range, resolution, and invalid-value representation (e.g. NaN allowed, sentinel value, separate validity flag) for every interface signal of the component, and choose data types and scaling consistent with that range plus a safety margin. Perform worst-case range analysis along the computation chain so intermediate types cannot overflow. State preconditions for numerically dangerous operations in the requirements (e.g. divisor guaranteed > epsilon, integrator reset on mode change) and decide where the check is enforced — producer, consumer, or both.

items.name: Performance / Accuracy reduced
items.description: Reduced numerical or control accuracy, e.g. due to rounding errors, fixed-point quantization, wrong filter/observer selection, insufficient sample rate, accumulated drift, or excessive latency in the dataflow.
items.measures: Specify accuracy requirements per interface signal if required (tolerance, max error, noise floor, drift). Allocate an end-to-end accuracy/error budget across the chain of components (sensor → filter → control → actuator) so each component has a defined slice. Define the component's sample/update rate consistent with the dynamics being observed or controlled (Nyquist plus margin, control bandwidth) and specify the computation and communication latency budget. Specify data type precision and intermediate width so rounding/quantization through the chain stays within the budget. Constrain algorithm choice in the requirements via filter/observer characteristics (bandwidth, phase margin, settling time, steady-state error). Identify where quantization or saturation occurs and place it where the information loss is acceptable.

items.name: Preemption and Statefulness related failures
items.description: Stateful logic is interrupted or re-entered at an unsafe point, so partially-updated internal state is observed or corrupted (e.g., ISR/task re-entrancy on shared state, torn or non-atomic multi-step updates, missing critical section around a commit, state lost or duplicated across cycles or mode switches).
items.measures: Define and document the reentrancy contract of every stateful function. For non-reentrant functions, ensure they are called from exactly one execution context and that the interrupting/preempting context does not touch their variables or buffers. Where preemption is unavoidable, protect the commit step with a critical section, atomic operation, or double-buffer/snapshot pattern so observers always see a consistent state.

items.name: Resource exhaustion / memory corruption
items.description: Resource or memory faults — stack overflow, heap fragmentation/exhaustion, buffer overflow/underflow, leak, file/handle/socket exhaustion, queue overflow — leading to incorrect behavior, denial of service, or loss of control state.
items.measures: Stack: monitor at runtime (RTOS/safety-OS stack checking, MPU guard pages) and measure worst-case stack usage statically. Heap: prefer no dynamic allocation in safety-critical paths; if used, bound it and use pools with quotas. Buffers: validate with static analysis tools and protect critical regions via MPU/MMU. For other resources (queues, handles, sockets), apply quotas, timeouts, and back-pressure.

items.name: Scaling / unit mismatch (internal)
items.description: Internal scaling or units are inconsistent across the implementation (e.g., fixed-point Q-format wrong, Nm vs %, deg vs rad, m vs ft, ms vs us), leading to incorrect results.
items.measures: Mostly covered by code review and unit testing. At architecture level, the relevant case is cross-component communication: ensure interface data types, units, and scaling are explicitly defined and consistently used by producer and consumer.

items.name: Stale data usage
items.description: Computation uses outdated or inconsistent data due to missing freshness, sequence, or timestamp checks (e.g., missed update, old sample reused, mixed-cycle signals, sensor data older than the control horizon).
items.measures: Relevant when components exchange data while running at different rates (e.g. 1 ms producer to 10 ms consumer, or async sensor publishing into a periodic controller). Detect when data is not produced or consumed within the expected interval (age check, sequence counter, timestamp). Size buffers and queues so they cannot silently drop or overrun.

items.name: State machine / mode management failure
items.description: Incorrect state transitions or mode handling: illegal state reached, wrong transition, failure to enter safe/degraded mode, state and mode out of sync between modules.
items.measures: Cover all defined transitions (and explicit handling of undefined ones) by review and test. Pay attention to restart paths: e.g. if the controller has a warm reset and persistent RAM is not reset to a defined value, the state machine may skip initialization and end up in an unexpected state. Ensure persistent state has integrity checks and a defined recovery action when invalid.

items.name: Synchronization failures
items.description: Coordination or ordering between tasks, threads, or distributed components is wrong (e.g., wrong sequencing or phase alignment, missing or incorrect handshake/event/trigger, missed notification or wake-up, lost startup event after restart).
items.measures: Example: a controller waits for a specific message on the communication bus to perform a self-test, but that message does not arrive after a warm restart because the sender has already moved past the trigger. Ensure required start-up events are reproduced after every kind of reset, or that recovery logic can synthesize the missing event.

items.name: Timing failures
items.description: The software function executes too late, too early, with too much jitter, or not within the deadline (missed deadline, schedule overrun, blocking call in real-time path).
items.measures: Core failure mode for timing problems in software, typically covered by program-flow monitoring combined with timing supervision and a hardware (external) watchdog. Establish worst-case execution time (WCET) bounds for safety-relevant tasks and verify them by measurement and/or static timing analysis.

items.name: Unintended activation
items.description: The software function activates when it should not (e.g., wrong mode gating, spurious state transition, incorrect enable conditions, false positive trigger).
items.measures: Example: entering a self-test or maintenance mode while the system is in an unsafe situation because a precondition (vehicle/aircraft/robot motion, payload state, operator presence) was not used as a gating condition. Define the full enable predicate for every action and verify each gate.

items.name: Watchdog/reset behavior unsafe
items.description: Watchdog, reset, or restart behavior is unsafe (reset triggered in a critical phase, reboot loop, outputs not forced to a safe state during restart, persistent fault state lost on reset).
items.measures: Distinguish the different reset sources (power-on reset, warm reset, watchdog reset, software reset, brown-out) and define how RAM data is treated for each (re-initialized, retained, cleared on integrity failure). Consider the operational context during reset (e.g. mid-flight, mid-motion, mid-procedure) and ensure outputs are commanded to a defined safe state during the unavailable window.

items.name: Wrong logic
items.description: Instead of the intended function the software executes wrong logic, e.g. instead of entering sleep/idle mode the software stays in run, or the wrong control law is selected for the current mode.
items.measures: Component specific failure mode.

items.name: Corrupted data / Integrity not checked
items.description: End-to-end protection (CRC, checksum, MAC, parity) fails or is not validated by the receiver, allowing corrupted data to be used.

items.name: Duplicate / replayed message
items.description: Old or duplicate messages are accepted as current (replay attack, gateway/router duplication, diagnostic or test tool injection, retried frames not deduplicated).

items.name: Endianness / bitfield packing error
items.description: Byte order, bit offsets, alignment, or packed-struct layout mismatch causes incorrect decoding/encoding of interface data.

items.name: Freshness / sequence failure
items.description: Receiver does not properly validate message freshness or order (missing timestamp/counter checks, rollover mishandled, out-of-sequence messages accepted, clock not synchronized between sender and receiver).

items.name: Initialization/default value misuse
items.description: Receiver uses uninitialized or default values before the first valid update arrives, or treats a default/invalid-marker value as valid without qualification.

items.name: Latency / jitter on interface
items.description: Variable or excessive interface delay breaks control assumptions (late arrival, bursty delivery, jitter not handled, queueing delay in middleware/network).

items.name: Missing signal / no update
items.description: Input or message is not received or stops updating (timeout, bus silent, publisher not sending, subscription not established, receiver not handling missing updates).

items.name: Out-of-range / implausible value
items.description: Received value is outside allowed bounds or implausible given other signals (range or plausibility checks missing or incorrect, cross-signal consistency not verified).

items.name: Output formatting error
items.description: Transmitted output is encoded incorrectly for the consumer (datatype, scale, units, or bit layout mismatch on transmit).

items.name: Output not updated / wrong update rate
items.description: Outputs are not published, are published at the wrong rate, or are published irregularly (scheduler or configuration mismatch), causing consumers to act on missing or late outputs.

items.name: Stuck-at / frozen value
items.description: Interface value repeats or freezes (last value held, sensor frozen, sender stuck) even though the underlying physical quantity changes.

items.name: Wrong datatypes
items.description: Data type mismatch at the interface (e.g., signed vs unsigned, float vs integer, wrong width, enum vs integer), causing misinterpretation.

items.name: Wrong enumeration value / invalid state code
items.description: Enum or state value is outside the allowed set (reserved or invalid codes), or the mapping of codes to meaning is wrong between sender and receiver.

items.name: Wrong scaling / units at interface
items.description: Encoding or decoding mismatch between sender and receiver (e.g., 0.1 Nm/bit vs 1 Nm/bit, deg vs rad, percent vs fraction, m vs ft) leading to systematic error.

items.name: Wrong sign / polarity
items.description: Signal polarity is inverted or sign convention differs between sender and receiver (active-low treated as active-high; torque, angle, or force sign inverted; coordinate frame flipped).

items.name: Wrong signal mapping / wrong ID
items.description: Wrong message or signal is connected or decoded (wrong bus message ID, wrong topic/port/service name, wrong port/bus element mapping, swapped channels in an I/O configuration).

items.name: Wrong source / channel swap
items.description: Data from an unintended sender, channel, or source is accepted (e.g. wrong ADC channel due to routing/config error, wrong sensor instance subscribed, wrong redundant lane selected).

enums.name: OccurrenceLevel
enums.description: Five-level estimate of how likely the design causes behind this malfunction are to be present over the product's service life, judged against the strength of the preventive measures in place (proven design, design rules, prior field experience). Design maturity and the amount of new technology or new design are the main drivers: novel, unproven design with weak prevention raises the likelihood; mature, well-proven design with strong prevention and field history lowers it. Higher level = more likely. Rated on the malfunction directly, as this profile has no separate cause concept. Occurrence covers only measures that change the design to make the cause less likely; measures that merely check an existing design to reveal whether the problem is present belong to detection, not occurrence. Do not credit the same measure to both axes.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — Very Low: cause very unlikely — mature, well-proven design reused unchanged, with strong preventive measures and extensive field experience
Level 2 — Low: cause unlikely — established design with only minor adaptations and effective prevention, backed by substantial prior experience
Level 3 — Medium: cause plausible — partially new design or moderate changes to a known concept, with some prevention and some prior experience
Level 4 — High: cause likely — significant new design or new technology, with limited prevention and little prior experience
Level 5 — Very High: cause very likely — novel technology or an unproven design concept, with weak or no preventive measures and no prior experience

enums.name: DetectionLevel
enums.description: Five-level estimate of the confidence that the verification measures reveal the potential design problem in the finished design before release (analysis, reviews, and testing). Higher level = weaker coverage and lower detection confidence. Detection covers only measures that check an existing design to reveal whether the problem is present; measures that change the design to make the cause less likely belong to occurrence, not detection. Do not credit the same measure to both axes.

permissibleValues.description: Level 1 — Proven: comprehensive verification covering all relevant operating conditions reveals the potential design problem with very high confidence
Level 2 — Good: strong verification covering the main operating conditions reveals the problem with high confidence, though not exhaustive over every condition
Level 3 — Moderate: standard analysis, review, and testing covering nominal and some boundary conditions; moderate confidence, corner cases may be missed
Level 4 — Limited: only basic reviews or limited checks performed; does not cover all operating conditions, so detection confidence is low
Level 5 — None: no effective verification measure to reveal the potential design problem; latent design faults can escape to operation

enums.name: TaskType
enums.description: Classification of the type of safety task.

permissibleValues.description: Safety measure implemented and active during operation (e.g. monitoring, diagnostics, fault reaction)
Safety measure applied during development (e.g. review, analysis, testing, design constraint)
Other task type not covered by the standard categories

sections.title: Question 1: Analysis Input sufficient?
paragraphs: Does the System Safety Analysis reflect the **current** System Design and System Architecture? Are all system elements and the interfaces between them listed in the Safety Analysis?
For each system element there should be a description of its main functions and its role in the overall system.

sections.title: Question 2: Are all relevant failure modes for the system covered?
paragraphs: The following list of potential failure modes does not need to be applied for every system element analysis. Instead, the **relevant failure modes shall be selected per element**. For those which are related to the overall architecture, provide an argument (for example, regarding the risk that several elements share a common resource, a redundancy or arbitration concept is in place).

sections.title: Question 3: Are the safety requirements linked?
paragraphs: The failure modes of an analysis should have a relation to the main System Safety Requirements. For example, if a system element does not deliver its specified function, what is the Safety Requirement which is violated?
It is **NOT sufficient** to just select an ASIL — the requirement which is related to the ASIL shall be linked.

sections.title: Question 4: Is the risk rating performed?
paragraphs: For System Safety Analysis there should be at least one risk rating documented describing the main aspects:
bullets: What is the **occurrence** of the failure scenarios, considering design maturity and the amount of new technology involved?
What are the **measures to prevent** this from occurring?
Are **further measures required** to monitor this scenario during operation?
sections.note: For interface failure modes it is NOT required to perform a risk rating. The risk rating is performed for the functional failure modes of a system element.

sections.title: Question 5: Are the tasks managed?
paragraphs: If during the safety analysis risk reduction tasks are defined related to dedicated operational measures (for example, additional monitoring) or development-time measures (for example, additional analysis or testing), then a ticket shall be created in the task tracking system to manage the tasks.

items.name: Loss of function
items.description: The system element does not provide its intended function at all (complete omission of the function when it is required), e.g. due to element unavailability, failure to start, or a blocked activation path.
items.measures: Define the required availability of the function and specify a defined system reaction to its loss (degraded mode, fail-safe state, redundancy or fallback element). Ensure the loss is detectable (heartbeat, alive-monitoring, plausibility of downstream effect) within the fault-tolerant time interval.

items.name: Unintended function / activation
items.description: The system element provides its function when it is not required, or activates without a valid command or precondition (spurious activation, wrong operating mode, unintended state transition).
items.measures: Define the full enable predicate (all preconditions and gating conditions) for every function and verify each gate. Where unintended activation is safety-relevant, add an independent confirmation or arbitration path so a single fault cannot trigger the function.

items.name: Incorrect function (wrong output/behavior)
items.description: The system element performs the intended function incorrectly — wrong value, wrong magnitude, wrong direction/sign, or wrong behavior for the current operating condition.
items.measures: Specify acceptance criteria and plausibility ranges for the element's output. Add monitoring, cross-checks, or redundant computation where an incorrect output is safety-relevant. Element-specific analysis is required to identify the credible incorrect behaviors.

items.name: Degraded performance / accuracy
items.description: The function is delivered but with reduced accuracy, resolution, range, or capacity (drift, reduced dynamic range, saturation, wear over lifetime), such that system-level requirements are no longer met.
items.measures: Allocate an end-to-end performance/accuracy budget across the contributing elements. Specify tolerances, drift limits, and lifetime effects per element and monitor for degradation where it is safety-relevant.

items.name: Timing / availability failure
items.description: The function is delivered too late, too early, intermittently, or not within its deadline (missed reaction time, excessive latency, intermittent dropout, startup or recovery too slow).
items.measures: Define the fault-tolerant time interval and the required reaction time at system level, and allocate timing budgets to each element. Supervise timing (watchdog, deadline monitoring, alive counters) and define the safe reaction when a timing violation is detected.

items.name: Mode / state management failure
items.description: Incorrect system mode or state handling: an illegal mode is reached, a required transition to a safe/degraded mode does not occur, or modes are inconsistent between cooperating elements.
items.measures: Define the complete set of system modes and their allowed transitions, including explicit handling of undefined transitions. Verify safe-state entry and mode consistency across elements, especially across restart, recovery, and reconfiguration paths.

items.name: Redundancy / arbitration failure
items.description: A redundancy or voting/arbitration concept does not work as intended (common-cause failure defeats redundancy, wrong lane selected, arbitration accepts a faulty source, degraded lane not detected).
items.measures: Analyze common-cause and dependent failures for redundant elements (shared power, clock, resource, environment). Ensure faulty lanes are detected and excluded, and that the arbitration/voting logic itself is monitored.

items.name: Shared-resource conflict
items.description: Multiple elements contend for a shared resource (power, bus bandwidth, memory, compute, actuator authority) leading to starvation, interference, or unintended coupling between otherwise independent functions.
items.measures: Identify shared resources and specify freedom-from-interference measures (resource budgeting, partitioning, quotas, priority/authority arbitration). Verify that a fault in one function cannot exhaust a resource needed by a safety-relevant function.

items.name: Environmental / operating-condition robustness
items.description: The element does not tolerate the specified operating conditions (temperature, vibration, EMC, voltage, contamination, ageing), leading to malfunction under foreseeable conditions.
items.measures: Specify the operating envelope and qualification conditions for each element. Verify robustness by analysis and environmental testing, and define behavior at and beyond the specified limits.

items.name: Initialization / recovery failure
items.description: The element is not correctly initialized or recovered (wrong startup state, dependencies started in the wrong order, persistent state not restored or not cleared, unsafe state after warm restart).
items.measures: Define the required initialization order and preconditions across cooperating elements. Distinguish reset/restart sources and define how persistent state is treated for each. Verify that outputs are held in a defined safe state during the unavailable window.

items.name: Systematic design fault (new technology / new design)
items.description: A latent systematic fault introduced by new technology, a novel design concept, or insufficiently validated requirements — the dominant occurrence driver in system-level FMEA.
items.measures: Increase the occurrence rating for new or unproven design and reduce it as experience and validation evidence accumulate. Apply additional analysis, prototyping, and verification proportional to the novelty of the design.

items.name: Missing signal / no update
items.description: An interface signal or message is not received or stops updating (timeout, silent source, link down, connection not established, receiver not handling the missing update).

items.name: Stuck-at / frozen value
items.description: An interface value repeats or freezes (last value held, source stuck) even though the underlying physical quantity changes.

items.name: Out-of-range / implausible value
items.description: A received value is outside allowed bounds or implausible given other signals (range or plausibility checks missing or incorrect, cross-signal consistency not verified).

items.name: Corrupted data / integrity not checked
items.description: End-to-end protection (CRC, checksum, MAC, parity) fails or is not validated by the receiver, allowing corrupted interface data to be used.

items.name: Freshness / sequence failure
items.description: The receiver does not properly validate message freshness or order (missing timestamp/counter checks, out-of-sequence messages accepted, duplicate or replayed messages).

items.name: Latency / jitter on interface
items.description: Variable or excessive interface delay breaks control or coordination assumptions (late arrival, bursty delivery, queueing delay).

items.name: Wrong scaling / units at interface
items.description: Encoding or decoding mismatch between sender and receiver (e.g. resolution per bit, deg vs rad, percent vs fraction, unit mismatch) leading to systematic error.

items.name: Wrong signal mapping / wrong source
items.description: The wrong message, signal, channel, or source is connected or decoded (wrong ID, swapped channels, wrong redundant lane, wrong instance subscribed).

items.name: Interface specification mismatch
items.description: Sender and receiver assume different interface definitions (datatype, semantics, valid range, invalid-value marker, or protocol version), causing misinterpretation.

H.label: High
H.description: Highest priority. Requires a mitigation, or an explicit rationale for the current severity/occurrence/detection combination.

M.label: Medium
M.description: Moderate priority. Review the rating and consider whether further risk reduction is worthwhile.

L.label: Low
L.description: Lower priority given the current rating. Still subject to normal review.
